extracted.intended_audience: applied mathematicians, theoretical physicists, engineers, and scientifically literate readers (e.g., readers of Engineering & Science)
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles and criteria for what applied mathematicians do, how they work, and what makes their work valuable — emphasizing interaction of mathematical analysis and physical ideas, pragmatic rigor, and contribution to knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of an applied mathematician
rubrics_metrics.description: Applied mathematician described by contrast with pure mathematician and physicist; captured by Rayleigh's view that methods 'present themselves naturally to a physicist' and by von Karman's quip that an applied mathematician 'assumes everything but the responsibility.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay emphasizes that the applied mathematician's identity is tied to working on physically motivated problems, often using methods natural to physicists rather than insisting on the uniform rigor of pure mathematics. (Includes von Karman's joking/deliberate definitions and Rayleigh's quoted passage about physicist-style methods.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary concern: understanding of nature / description of physical phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘It is with the understanding of nature that applied mathematics is primarily, if not wholly, concerned.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied mathematicians typically describe physical phenomena in terms of known physical laws (e.g., mechanics, Navier–Stokes), focusing on capturing and explaining behavior rather than on discovering new fundamental laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary job: generation of new physical ideas via mathematical investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary job of the applied mathematician is 'the generation of new physical ideas through mathematical investigations.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical work should produce conceptual/physical insight as well as (or even instead of) raw numerical predictions. Cites Lighthill and supports the view that analysis can reveal ideas not evident beforehand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical analysis should illuminate physical aspects, not only produce numeric predictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoting Truesdell and Toupin: 'The developments must illumine the physical aspects of the theory, not necessarily in the narrower sense of prediction of numerical results for comparison with experimental measurement, but rather for the grasp and picture of the theory in relation to experience.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate applied-math work on how well it produces an intelligible physical picture and clarifies the relation between theory and experience; pursuing or avoiding complexity is permissible insofar as it serves this illumination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic attitude to rigor (physicist-style sufficiency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rayleigh: pure mathematician may complain of 'deficient rigor' but 'the physicist may occasionally do well to rest content with arguments which are fairly satisfactory and conclusive from his point of view.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied work may legitimately accept less-than-pure-mathematical rigor when the arguments are conclusive for physical purposes. The essay frames this as a trade-off: maintain high standards where needed, but accept pragmatic arguments that illuminate phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribution criterion: adding something to knowledge and enabling others
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardy's claim about what makes work worth doing: 'that I have added something to knowledge, and helped others to add more; and that these somethings have a value which differs in degree only, and not in kind, from that of ... other artists ... who have left some kind of memorial behind them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess applied-math work by its contribution to knowledge and its utility in helping others make further advances; value includes a notion of permanence and lasting intellectual contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curiosity and knowledge-as-good-in-itself motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Housman's statement that 'Curiosity, the desire to know things as they are, is a craving no less native to the being of man ...' and that 'The acquisition of knowledge needs no such justification.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied mathematics can be justified on intrinsic grounds of curiosity and the desire to understand; this is a legitimate evaluative lens separate from utilitarian or aesthetic justifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/disciplinary continuity with physical problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Applied mathematics is historically rooted in solving real physical problems (e.g., Euler, the Bernoullis, vibrating-string debates among Euler, Bernoulli, D'Alembert, Lagrange).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work should be conscious of this tradition: addressing concrete physical questions and building on classical frameworks (mechanics, continuum models) is characteristic and valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness of equations beyond original hypotheses as a mark of success
rubrics_metrics.description: David Gilbarg: 'equations have often been successful beyond the limits of their original hypotheses, and indeed this type of success is one of the hallmarks of a great theory.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate theories/models for their ability to predict or describe phenomena outside the strict domain of their derivation; robustness and far-reaching applicability count positively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role distinctions: applied mathematician vs theoretical physicist vs pure mathematician
rubrics_metrics.description: A practical distinction is that theoretical physicists often seek new physical laws, while applied mathematicians describe phenomena using established laws; pure mathematicians prioritize internal rigor and abstraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use role-aware criteria when judging work: measure against appropriate goals (discovery vs description vs abstraction), recognizing boundaries are not sharp and cross-fertilization occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical problem-solving style: value of physical intuition and parsimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Anecdote (locomotives and the deer fly): physicist's quick physical-reasoning solution (time × speed) versus mathematician's summing of a series; von Neumann's instant answer '50 miles' (but 'I only had to sum a series').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prize solutions that use physical insight and parsimony when appropriate; beware of overformalizing problems where simple physical reasoning suffices, while recognizing formal derivations also have value.
